name: ARCHROCK

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: My correction may go too far in the other direction. Maintenance capital expenditure of $125-135M is a management-defined non-GAAP number and it is less than HALF of $286M of depreciation and amortisation on a fleet of rotating equipment that genuinely wears out. If true economic sustaining capex is nearer D&A, the base falls from about $600M to about $435M, the market's implied growth rises from -1.3% to +6.7%, and Archrock stops looking fair and starts looking demanding — because a company whose adjusted EBITDA was FLAT year over year has to find that 6.7% somewhere. The Q2 print is the bear's best evidence: flat EBITDA in a market management calls 'structurally tight', while spending $250-275M a year.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Maintenance capital expenditure as a share of depreciation over several years, and whether the compression fleet's average age rises. More directly: 2027 adjusted EBITDA against 2026's $865-885M, which is the return on the growth capital already spent. If $250-275M a year buys no EBITDA growth, the growth programme is not earning its cost of capital and the sustaining base with zero growth is the generous reading, not the conservative one.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, and it is the reason I underwrite zero rather than a positive number. Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $212.6M against $212.7M is flat despite the NGCS acquisition and two years of heavy growth capital, and the full-year top end was cut by $30M. That is not what a compounding growth programme looks like in-period. It does not settle the question — compression revenue arrives on multi-year contracts with a lag from the capital — but it means the burden of proof sits with the bull.
devils_advocate.unresolved: I could not reconcile the engine's $150.9M base to the 10-Q cash flow statement line by line, so I know the base is depressed by growth capex but not precisely by how much of it versus working capital and cash interest. I also could not obtain any independent view of contract renewal pricing or the order book beyond management's own characterisation, and there was no company-specific news in the store for 90 days to corroborate it.

what_changed: Nothing that invalidates the model, but the Q2 release (2026-08-05) supplies the numbers that dismantle the engine's reading. Adjusted EBITDA flat year over year at $212.6M; full-year 2026 guidance TIGHTENED to $865-885M from $865-915M; growth capital expenditures reaffirmed at $250-275M and maintenance capital expenditures guided at $125-135M separately; multi-year growth capex guidance of $1.4-1.6B introduced for 2027-2030. Quarterly depreciation and amortisation is $71.5M, about $286M annualised. The NGCS acquisition closed in Q2 2025 for $296.6M of cash net of cash acquired — an acquisition INSIDE the three-year cash-flow window, which is part of why the FCF series is as lumpy as it is. The 6.250% senior notes due 2028 were redeemed in full on 2026-04-01. No company-specific news is in the store for the last 90 days, which lowers my confidence that nothing else happened rather than confirming it; the sector feed is all oil-price and OPEC+ macro, with Brent above $100.
consensus_case: Archrock is the largest US contract natural-gas compression owner, renting horsepower to producers and midstream operators on multi-year contracts. At $32.96 it carries a $5.8B market capitalisation and roughly $8.1B of enterprise value against guided 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $865-885M — about 9.3x. The bull case is a structurally tight compression market, high utilisation, a healthy order book and durable natural-gas demand; the price already embeds it. The case for the price rather than above it: adjusted EBITDA in Q2 2026 was $212.6M against $212.7M a year earlier, essentially FLAT, and the company tightened full-year guidance by cutting the top end from $915M to $885M on make-ready costs, lube oil, weaker aftermarket demand and higher incentive compensation. Archrock has committed to $250-275M of growth capital this year and $1.4-1.6B cumulatively across 2027-2030, so this is a capital-hungry business whose current earnings are flat while it spends; a 9.3x multiple is a normal, not a generous, price for that.
base_case_rationale: The engine's $150.9M FCFF base is CFO less TOTAL capital expenditure, and total capex here is $375-410M of which only $125-135M is maintenance. So the base charges Archrock the full cost of expanding its fleet and then the reverse DCF applies a growth rate to what is left — the same dollar counted twice, once as a cost and once as the growth it buys. This is the exact mirror of the CTOS, ALTG and WLFC rental-capex bug: there growth capex was MISSING from capex and manufactured false cheapness; here it is fully captured and misread as sustaining, manufacturing false richness. Corrected, the base is the cash the EXISTING fleet throws off: EBITDA of about $875M less maintenance capex of $130M, taxed — roughly $600M of sustaining FCFF, four times the engine's number. The consistent pairing for that base is ZERO growth, because I have removed the investment that would produce growth. On $600M and 0% the market implies -1.3%, and the fair value lands at about $34.50 against a $32.96 price. Two independent methods therefore agree that Archrock is close to fairly valued: a sustaining-cash-flow DCF at roughly no growth, and a 9.3x EV/EBITDA multiple that sits squarely in the range where contract compression peers trade.
key_risks: The -81.6% gap, the +34.2% implied growth and the 12th-percentile Energy cohort rank are ALL artifacts of growth capital expenditure being netted out of the FCFF base and then implicitly re-added as required growth; the engine's fair value of $6.05 prices Archrock's entire equity at under 1x EBITDA and should be disregarded

The correction is not free: it depends on management's maintenance capex definition of $125-135M against $286M of D&A, and at a D&A-based sustaining capex the market's implied growth rises to +6.7% against flat current EBITDA
Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was flat year over year and full-year guidance was tightened by cutting the top end $30M on make-ready costs, lube oil and weak aftermarket demand

The NGCS acquisition ($296.6M cash, Q2 2025) sits inside the three-year cash-flow window, so the FCF series of $11.6M / $70.6M / $119.6M compares different companies and the peak-cycle flag reads off that discontinuity
$1.4-1.6B of growth capital committed for 2027-2030 against a $5.8B equity: the thesis on this name is really a thesis about the return on that capital, which is unobservable today
No company-specific news in the store for 90 days, so my read on contract pricing rests entirely on management's own characterisation
watch_for: 2027 adjusted EBITDA guidance against 2026's $865-885M — the first clean read on the return earned by the 2025-26 growth capital
Maintenance capital expenditure trending toward the $286M depreciation run rate, which would confirm the base is nearer $435M than $600M
Fleet utilisation and the order book, and whether the make-ready cost pressure cited in Q2 persists into the second half
Any further tightening or cut to the growth capex plan, which would signal management's own read on the cycle
